question: What documentation standards does PL 2338/2023 set for high-risk AI systems in a financial institution?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20(I) requires, for high-risk systems, documentation in a format adequate to the development process and technology used, covering the system's functioning and the decisions involved in its construction, implementation, and use across all relevant lifecycle stages (design, development, evaluation, operation, discontinuation). Art. 19(2) requires this technical documentation to be prepared before market availability or service use and kept updated during use. Unlike the EU AI Act, which prescribes detailed technical-documentation content in Annex IV, PL 2338 states the documentation obligation at a higher level of generality, leaving format to be adequate to the technology. A financial institution must maintain current lifecycle documentation for each high-risk system.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Contrast with EU Annex IV specificity is interpretive.

question: How must human-AI interaction be designed for a high-risk lending system under PL 2338/2023 to ensure effective human oversight?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20 sole paragraph requires that human oversight of high-risk systems enable the responsible persons to: understand the system's capacities and limitations and control its functioning so anomalies are identified and resolved quickly (I); be aware of automation bias and the tendency to over-rely on outputs (II); correctly interpret outputs given the system's characteristics and available interpretation tools (III); decide in any specific situation not to use the system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output (IV); and intervene in or interrupt operation (V). Art. 11 additionally requires significant human involvement and a final human determination for irreversible impacts. For a lending system, the human-AI interface must be designed so a loan officer can meaningfully understand, question, override, and halt the system — not merely rubber-stamp its output.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] sole-paragraph items I-V.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 require managing changes to a deployed high-risk AI system?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 25 requires the algorithmic impact assessment to be a continuous iterative process throughout the high-risk system's lifecycle, with periodic updates. Art. 25(1) leaves update periodicity to the competent authority's regulation, and Art. 25(2) requires public participation in updates. Art. 19(1) confirms that governance measures apply across the whole lifecycle from conception to discontinuation. Art. 24(5) requires notification of unexpected post-deployment risks. For change management, a financial institution must re-assess and update the impact assessment and documentation when the system, its data, or its context materially changes, and notify authorities and affected persons of newly identified risks.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 apply to a RegTech AI system used for automated regulatory-compliance monitoring in a bank?
ground_truth: RegTech AI for compliance monitoring is not enumerated among the high-risk purposes in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, so it is not automatically high-risk. The provider must perform and document a preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13), and the general governance measures of Art. 19 apply (transparency, bias mitigation, data-protection legitimation, information security). If the RegTech system makes or informs decisions with relevant legal effects on individuals, the Chapter II rights (explanation, contestation, human review) attach. Where the system's outputs affect access to essential services or credit, it could cross into high-risk under Art. 17(IV) or (V); the competent authority may also designate it under Art. 18. Absent that, RegTech is subject to baseline preliminary assessment and general governance.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What must a Brazilian bank consider under PL 2338/2023 when procuring a third-party high-risk AI system?
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023, a bank procuring a third-party AI system becomes its operator (operador, Art. 4(III)) while the vendor is the provider (fornecedor, Art. 4(II)); both are AI agents sharing governance duties to the extent of their roles. For a high-risk system, the bank as operator must ensure the Art. 19 general measures and Art. 20 enhanced measures are met — including lifecycle documentation, operation-logging, reliability testing, bias mitigation, and explainability — which requires obtaining adequate information and cooperation from the vendor. The bank must also ensure a preliminary assessment (Art. 13) and, for high-risk systems, an algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22) are conducted. Because strict liability attaches to high-risk systems (Art. 27(1)), procurement contracts should allocate documentation, testing, and information-sharing responsibilities to enable the bank's compliance.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] operador duties; contractual allocation is good practice.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 require interpretability of a high-risk credit model's outputs?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20(V) requires providers/operators of high-risk systems to adopt technical measures enabling the explainability of results and to make available general information on the AI model's functioning, explaining the logic and relevant criteria for producing results, and — upon the interested party's request — to provide adequate information allowing interpretation of the concretely produced results, respecting industrial and commercial secrecy. On the individual-rights side, Art. 8 lets an affected person request an explanation of a specific decision, including the rationale and logic, the AI's contribution level, the data and criteria applied to them, and the contestation mechanisms. For a high-risk credit model, interpretability must be provided both at the general model level (Art. 20(V)) and at the individual-decision level (Art. 8), balanced against trade-secret protection.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 20(V) trade-secret balancing.

question: How can a Brazilian financial institution demonstrate AI governance maturity under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 30(2) describes a mature governance program that, at minimum: demonstrates commitment to compliance and non-maleficence and proportionality; is adapted to the structure, scale, and volume of operations and their harm potential; aims to establish a trust relationship with affected persons through transparent action and participation mechanisms; is integrated into the general governance structure and establishes internal and external oversight; includes response plans to reverse harmful outcomes; and is continuously updated based on continuous monitoring and periodic evaluation. Combined with the Art. 19 baseline governance measures, these elements define maturity. Art. 30(3) rewards such maturity as an indicator of good faith mitigating sanctions. A financial institution demonstrates maturity by implementing and evidencing these program elements.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 30(2) sub-items.

category: AI Risk Context — Credit Decision Appeal
question: What rights does a Brazilian consumer have to appeal an automated credit decision under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 gives affected consumers strong appeal rights over automated credit decisions. Art. 9 grants the right to contest and request review of decisions producing relevant legal effects or significantly affecting interests, including a right to correct incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated data (Art. 9(1)) and to contest decisions based on discriminatory, unreasonable, or bad-faith inferences (Art. 9(2)). Art. 10 grants the right to request human intervention or review where the decision produces relevant legal effects or significantly affects interests, including through profiling; if human intervention is provably impossible, the operator must implement effective alternative re-analysis measures (Art. 10 sole paragraph). Art. 8 supports these by requiring an explanation of the decision. For an automated loan denial, the consumer can demand an explanation, contest the decision and underlying data, and request human review.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 9/10 paragraph structure.

question: How should a Brazilian securities firm track the performance of an investment AI under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Because investment/robo-advisory AI is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, the enhanced Art. 20 monitoring duties (including automatic operation-logging under Art. 20(II)) apply only if the system is classified high-risk via Art. 18 designation. For a non-high-risk investment AI, the general governance measures of Art. 19 apply, including adequate data-management and information-security measures across the lifecycle (Art. 19(1)), and a documented preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13). Where the system affects investors' interests, the Chapter II rights (explanation, contestation, human review) attach. So performance tracking rests on general governance and documented assessment unless the system is designated high-risk, in which case Art. 20(II) logging and Art. 25 continuous impact assessment apply.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] conditional application of Art. 20.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 promote equity and prevent discriminatory outcomes in lending AI?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 addresses equity through rights and governance measures. Art. 12 guarantees affected persons fair and isonomic treatment and prohibits AI systems causing direct, indirect, illegal, or abusive discrimination, including through sensitive-data use, disproportionate impacts based on personal characteristics, or apparently neutral criteria disadvantaging vulnerable groups. Art. 20(IV) requires high-risk systems to adopt bias-mitigation data-management measures, including bias evaluation with corrective measures to avoid perpetuating structural social biases, and an inclusive, diversity-oriented development team. Art. 9(2) lets persons contest decisions based on discriminatory inferences. For lending AI, the institution must test for and mitigate discriminatory outcomes, and affected persons can contest biased decisions. This parallels EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f) bias examination.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 20(IV) sub-items.

question: How must a Brazilian bank communicate AI-related risks to affected persons under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 requires risk communication both individually and publicly. Individually, Art. 7 requires clear and adequate prior information to affected persons about, among other things, the automated character of the decision, a general description of the system and the consequences of its use, the governance measures adopted, the categories of personal data used, and the security, non-discrimination, and reliability measures adopted including accuracy, precision, and coverage (Art. 7(VI)). Publicly, Art. 26 requires the conclusions of the algorithmic impact assessment to be public (safeguarding trade secrets), including residual risk. Art. 24(1)(i) requires public transparency about residual risks, especially where there is high potential harm to health or safety. A bank must therefore inform affected persons of the system's risks and publish impact-assessment conclusions.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 7 item numbering.

question: A Brazilian bank uses AI to assess mortgage applications. How is this classified and governed under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Mortgage-application assessment AI evaluates a natural person's debt capacity and creditworthiness, so it falls within PL 2338/2023 Art. 17(V) — 'evaluation of the debt-capacity of natural persons or establishment of their credit classification' — and is high-risk. High-risk classification triggers: the enhanced governance measures of Art. 20 (lifecycle documentation, operation-logging, reliability testing, bias mitigation, explainability, human oversight); a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22) following the Art. 24 methodology; strict civil liability (Art. 27(1)); and the affected-person rights of Chapter II (information, explanation, contestation, human review). The bank must complete a preliminary assessment (Art. 13), conduct the impact assessment, notify the competent authority, and publish the assessment conclusions (Art. 26).
notes: Mortgage clearly within Art. 17(V) debt-capacity/credit.

question: How must a Brazilian bank track and respond to emergent risks in high-risk AI after deployment under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 requires ongoing post-deployment risk tracking. Art. 25 makes the algorithmic impact assessment a continuous iterative process across the lifecycle with periodic updates. Art. 24(5) requires agents who become aware of unexpected risks to natural persons' rights after market introduction to immediately notify the competent authority and affected persons. Art. 20(II)'s automatic operation-logging supports detecting accuracy degradation and emergent discriminatory effects. If an emergent risk rises to a serious incident, Art. 31 requires communication to the authority within a reasonable period, and the authority may order corrective measures. For a high-risk system, the bank must continuously monitor, update its impact assessment, and escalate emergent risks through the notification and incident channels.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 handle cross-border AI governance for a multinational bank operating in Brazil?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 1 establishes national general rules for AI systems in Brazil, applying to development, implementation, and use of AI in the country. The bill does not contain an explicit extraterritoriality clause equivalent to the Korean AI Basic Act Art. 4(1); its reach is tied to AI activity affecting the Brazilian market and persons. For a multinational bank, systems used in Brazil are subject to PL 2338 regardless of where developed. Art. 32 (sole paragraph, item V) tasks the competent authority with international cooperation, and Art. 34 requires coordination with sectoral regulators. A multinational should map which of its AI systems touch Brazilian customers, apply PL 2338 to those, and reconcile obligations with other jurisdictions' frameworks (EU, Korea). ⚠VERIFY whether the Senate text added an explicit extraterritoriality provision.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] extraterritoriality; the consolidated text may differ. Flag for author.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 treat AI used for customer segmentation and marketing by a Brazilian bank?
ground_truth: Customer-segmentation and marketing AI is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, so it is not automatically high-risk. A documented preliminary risk assessment is required (Art. 13). The non-discrimination protections of Art. 12 apply: segmentation must not cause direct, indirect, illegal, or abusive discrimination, including disproportionate impacts based on personal characteristics or disadvantaging vulnerable groups through apparently neutral criteria. If segmentation feeds decisions affecting access to credit or essential services, it could cross into Art. 17(IV)/(V) high-risk territory. Where segmentation significantly affects individuals, Chapter II rights may apply. Absent high-risk status, the key constraints are the Art. 12 anti-discrimination rules and general governance under Art. 19.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 enable a response to systemic risks arising from widespread financial AI use?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 provides several levers for systemic-risk response. Art. 3(XI) establishes prevention, precaution, and mitigation of systemic risks as a principle. Art. 18 empowers the competent authority to designate systems as high-risk based on criteria including large-scale implementation (number of persons affected, geographic extent, duration, frequency) and high harm potential — enabling regulatory response to systemically significant financial AI. Art. 36 gives the authority sanctioning powers including suspension of a system's operation (Art. 36(V)) and preventive measures (Art. 36(2)) where there is risk of irreparable harm. Art. 34's coordination with sectoral (financial) regulators supports a joint systemic response. The bill thus relies on the authority's designation, supervision, and suspension powers rather than a dedicated financial-stability mechanism.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 36 item numbering.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 require measuring the impact of an AI system on affected customers?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 24(1) requires the algorithmic impact assessment to record, among other things: the probability of adverse consequences, including the number of persons potentially impacted (Art. 24(1)(c)); the severity of adverse consequences, including the effort needed to mitigate them (Art. 24(1)(d)); and the process and results of tests and evaluations and mitigation measures to verify possible rights impacts, with special emphasis on potential discriminatory impacts (Art. 24(1)(f)). For a financial institution, measuring customer impact means quantifying how many customers a high-risk system affects, how severe adverse outcomes could be, and testing specifically for discriminatory effects, all documented in the impact assessment.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] sub-item lettering.

question: Does PL 2338/2023 require or encourage an internal AI ethics committee at a financial institution?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not mandate a specifically named internal AI ethics committee (unlike the Korean AI Basic Act Art. 28, which addresses private autonomous AI ethics committees). Instead, Art. 19 requires AI agents to establish governance structures and internal processes ensuring system security and affected persons' rights, and Art. 30(2)(d) provides that a governance program should be integrated into the general governance structure and establish internal and external oversight mechanisms. A financial institution may implement an ethics or AI review committee as part of these required governance structures; doing so, as part of a code of good practice and governance, can serve as an indicator of good faith mitigating sanctions (Art. 30(3)). So an ethics committee is encouraged as good governance practice rather than statutorily mandated.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Contrast with Korean Art. 28 is accurate.

category: AI Risk Context — Open Banking AI
question: How does PL 2338/2023 apply to AI systems operating within Brazil's open-banking ecosystem?
ground_truth: Open-banking AI is not itself enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17; classification depends on the AI's function. If the AI evaluates debt capacity or credit (Art. 17(V)) using open-banking data, it is high-risk; if it merely aggregates or shares data, it may be lower-risk subject to preliminary assessment (Art. 13). Regardless of risk tier, the data-protection governance measure of Art. 19(IV) requires legitimation of data processing under the LGPD, including privacy by design and data minimization, and Art. 5(VI) guarantees affected persons' data-protection rights. Given open banking's reliance on personal-data sharing, LGPD compliance is central. The institution must classify each open-banking AI by function and apply high-risk obligations where credit evaluation is involved.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Function-dependent classification.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 protect vulnerable populations affected by financial AI?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 provides specific protections for vulnerable groups. Art. 7(3) requires AI systems directed at vulnerable groups — such as children, adolescents, the elderly, and persons with disabilities — to be developed so those persons can understand the system's functioning and their rights. Art. 12(II) prohibits discrimination that establishes disadvantages or aggravates the vulnerability of persons in a specific group, even through apparently neutral criteria. Art. 14(II) prohibits (as excessive risk) AI that exploits vulnerabilities of specific groups (e.g., by age or disability) to induce harmful behavior. Art. 18(IV) makes effect on a vulnerable group a criterion for high-risk designation. For financial AI, this means heightened care in design, disclosure, and non-discrimination when systems affect vulnerable customers.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] item references.

question: How should a Brazilian financial group monitor a portfolio of high-risk AI systems on an ongoing basis under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 25 requires the algorithmic impact assessment for each high-risk system to be a continuous iterative process across the lifecycle, with periodic updates whose periodicity the competent authority regulates. Art. 20(II) requires automatic operation-logging for high-risk systems, enabling ongoing assessment of accuracy and robustness and detection of discriminatory potential. Across a portfolio, a financial group must maintain continuous impact assessments and operation logs for each high-risk system, update them periodically and upon material change (Art. 24(5) for emergent risks), and ensure each system's documentation stays current (Art. 19(2)). The bill's monitoring is per-system; portfolio-level oversight is an organizational overlay on these per-system duties.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 enable tracking of a financial institution's AI compliance by regulators?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 gives the competent authority oversight tools. Art. 32 (sole paragraph) empowers it to oversee disclosure of information under Arts. 7 and 43, inspect and apply sanctions through due process (item IX), and request information from entities developing or using AI (item X). Art. 22 sole paragraph requires notification of high-risk systems by sharing preliminary and impact assessments. Art. 43 requires the authority to maintain a public database of high-risk AI impact-assessment documents, enabling public and regulatory tracking. Art. 34 coordinates with sectoral regulators. For a financial institution, compliance is tracked through mandatory notifications, the public impact-assessment database, and the authority's inspection and information-request powers.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 32 item numbering.

category: AI Risk Context — Stress Testing AI
question: How does PL 2338/2023 apply to AI used for financial stress-testing and risk modeling within a bank?
ground_truth: AI used for internal financial stress-testing and risk modeling is not enumerated as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, as it does not directly evaluate individuals' credit, employment, or access to essential services. It is therefore subject to the baseline regime: a documented preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13) and the general governance measures of Art. 19 (data management, information security, documentation). Because such systems typically do not produce decisions with direct legal effects on individual customers, the Chapter II individual-rights provisions may have limited application. If stress-testing outputs feed into decisions affecting individuals' credit access, the downstream credit system would be high-risk under Art. 17(V). Absent that, stress-testing AI is lower-risk under the bill.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What does PL 2338/2023 require when a financial institution retires or discontinues an AI system?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 19(1) provides that governance measures apply across the entire lifecycle, including the cessation of activities and discontinuation (encerramento de suas atividades e descontinuação), and Art. 20(I) requires documentation covering the discontinuation stage for high-risk systems. Art. 21(2), in the public-power context and instructive generally, requires discontinuation where the risks identified in the algorithmic impact assessment cannot be eliminated or substantively mitigated. For a financial institution retiring an AI system, this implies documenting the discontinuation decision and process, and mandatorily discontinuing high-risk systems whose unmitigable risks to rights are identified. The bill treats retirement as a governed lifecycle stage, not an unregulated end.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 21(2) scope.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 accommodate small financial institutions or fintechs in its governance requirements?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 provides proportionality accommodations for smaller entities. Art. 32 (final paragraph) allows the competent authority to establish differentiated conditions, requirements, and communication channels for providers and operators qualified as micro or small enterprises (under Complementary Law 123/2006) and startups (under Complementary Law 182/2021). Art. 30(2)(b) provides that governance programs should be adapted to the structure, scale, and volume of operations and their harm potential. The Art. 3(XII) proportionality principle reinforces this. So while the substantive high-risk obligations still apply to a small fintech's credit-scoring AI, the authority may tailor procedural requirements, and governance programs scale to the institution's size. This resembles proportionality accommodations in other frameworks.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] SME/startup provision wording.

question: How should a Brazilian bank integrate PL 2338/2023 AI governance with its existing enterprise risk and compliance functions?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 30(2)(d) provides that a governance program should be integrated into the entity's general governance structure and establish and apply internal and external oversight mechanisms. Art. 19 requires governance structures and internal processes across the AI lifecycle. Art. 34 requires the AI competent authority to coordinate with sectoral regulators, implying that a bank's AI governance should interface with existing financial-sector supervision rather than operate in isolation. For enterprise integration, a bank should embed AI-specific governance (preliminary assessments, impact assessments, high-risk controls) within its existing enterprise risk management, model risk management, and compliance functions, ensuring internal and external oversight as Art. 30(2)(d) requires.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What must a Brazilian bank publish about its high-risk credit AI's impact assessment under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 26 requires that, safeguarding industrial and commercial secrets, the conclusions of the algorithmic impact assessment be public, containing at least: (I) a description of the intended purpose, context of use, and territorial and temporal scope; (II) the risk-mitigation measures and the residual risk level after those measures; and (III) a description of the participation of affected segments, if any (per Art. 24(3)). Art. 43 requires the competent authority to create and maintain a public database of high-risk AI impact-assessment documents. For a high-risk credit AI, the bank must publish these impact-assessment conclusions and they will be accessible via the authority's public database, while trade secrets remain protected.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 26 items.

question: What are the detailed human-oversight obligations for a high-risk lending AI under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20 sole paragraph requires that human oversight of high-risk systems seek to prevent or minimize risks to rights and freedoms, enabling responsible persons to: (I) understand the system's capacities and limitations and duly control its functioning so anomalies and unexpected performance are identified and resolved quickly; (II) be aware of automation and over-reliance bias; (III) correctly interpret outputs given the system's characteristics and available tools; (IV) decide, in any specific situation, not to use the high-risk system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output; and (V) intervene in or interrupt the system's operation. Art. 10 grants affected persons the right to request human intervention/review, and Art. 11 requires significant human involvement and final human determination for irreversible impacts. For lending, these establish that human overseers must be trained, empowered, and able to override or halt the system.
legal_basis: PL 2338/2023 Art. 20 sole paragraph; Art. 10; Art. 11
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] sole-paragraph items I-V.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 translate ethical principles into practical governance obligations for financial AI?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 connects principles to practice through its governance chapter. The Art. 3 principles (human oversight, non-discrimination, transparency, explainability, auditability, reliability, accountability, precaution, non-maleficence, proportionality) are operationalized as concrete duties: transparency and explainability become Arts. 7-8 rights and Art. 20(V) measures; non-discrimination becomes Art. 12 and Art. 20(IV) bias mitigation; human oversight becomes Arts. 10-11 and Art. 20 sole paragraph; accountability becomes Art. 20(II) logging and Art. 27 liability. Art. 30 lets agents adopt codes of good practice and governance programs embodying these principles, with Art. 30(3) rewarding voluntary adherence as good faith. Ethics integration thus means implementing the specific Chapter II-IV obligations that give effect to the Art. 3 principles.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 govern data sharing by AI systems in open-banking contexts?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 governs AI data sharing primarily through its interface with data-protection law. Art. 19(IV) requires legitimation of data processing under the LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018), including privacy by design and by default and techniques minimizing personal-data use, as a general governance measure. Art. 5(VI) guarantees affected persons the right to privacy and personal-data protection. Art. 42(3) provides that text-and-data-mining activities involving personal data are subject to the LGPD. In open banking, where AI systems share and process personal financial data, the institution must ensure LGPD-compliant legal bases, data minimization, and the Art. 9(1) rights to correct, anonymize, block, or eliminate data. PL 2338 layers AI-specific governance on top of the LGPD's data-sharing rules rather than replacing them.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] LGPD cross-references.

question: How does PL 2338/2023 encourage a strong AI risk culture within a financial institution?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 fosters AI risk culture through governance programs and incentives. Art. 30(2) describes governance programs demonstrating organizational commitment to compliance, non-maleficence, and proportionality, integrated into the general governance structure with internal and external oversight and continuous updating. Art. 20(IV)(b) requires, for high-risk systems, an inclusive, diversity-oriented development team, embedding cultural values in system design. Art. 30(3) and Art. 36(1) reward good-faith governance culture — adoption of impact assessments, ethics codes, and corrective measures — as mitigating factors for sanctions. A financial institution builds AI risk culture by implementing these governance programs, diverse teams, and continuous-improvement practices, which are recognized and rewarded by the sanctioning regime.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What vendor due-diligence does PL 2338/2023 imply for a bank acquiring a high-risk AI system?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 does not prescribe a detailed vendor due-diligence checklist, but its allocation of duties implies substantial diligence. As operator (Art. 4(III)) of a high-risk third-party system, the bank remains bound by the Art. 20 enhanced governance measures (documentation, logging, reliability testing, bias mitigation, explainability, human oversight), which it can only satisfy with adequate information and cooperation from the provider. Because strict liability attaches to high-risk systems (Art. 27(1)) to the extent of each agent's participation, the bank must diligence the vendor's compliance capability, obtain technical documentation, and secure contractual commitments on testing, logging, and information-sharing. Due diligence thus flows from the operator's non-delegable Art. 20 obligations and the shared strict-liability exposure.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Due-diligence detail is inferred from operator duties.

question: When does PL 2338/2023 require external independent assessment of a high-risk AI system?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 Art. 23 requires the algorithmic impact assessment to be conducted by a professional or team with the necessary technical, scientific, and legal knowledge and functional independence (independência funcional). By default this independence can be internal. However, the sole paragraph of Art. 23 empowers the competent authority to regulate the cases in which the impact assessment, or its audit, must necessarily be conducted by a professional or team external to the provider. So external independent assessment is not universally required but can be mandated by the competent authority for specified categories of high-risk systems. A financial institution should monitor authority regulations to determine whether its high-risk systems fall into an externally-audited category.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 23 sole-paragraph.

question: Under what conditions could algorithmic-trading AI become high-risk under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: Algorithmic-trading AI is not listed as high-risk in PL 2338/2023 Art. 17, but Art. 18 empowers the competent authority to add systems to the high-risk list based on at least one of several criteria, of which the following are relevant to algorithmic trading: large-scale implementation considering the number of persons affected and geographic extent, duration, and frequency (Art. 18(I)); potential to negatively impact the exercise of rights or use of a service (Art. 18(II)); and high potential for material harm (Art. 18(III)). Combined with the Art. 3(XI) systemic-risk principle, these criteria could justify designating high-frequency or systemically significant trading AI as high-risk. Until such designation, algorithmic trading is subject to preliminary assessment (Art. 13) and general governance (Art. 19). The answer identifies the Art. 18 designation pathway.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 18 criteria numbering.

question: What must a Brazilian bank disclose to a customer subject to an AI-assisted credit decision under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 requires layered disclosure. Under Art. 5(I) and Art. 7, before contracting or use the customer must receive clear, adequate prior information about: the automated character of the interaction and decision (Art. 7(I)); a general description of the system, its decisions, and consequences (Art. 7(II)); the operators and governance measures (Art. 7(III)); the role of AI and humans in the decision (Art. 7(IV)); the categories of personal data used (Art. 7(V)); and the security, non-discrimination, and reliability measures including accuracy, precision, and coverage (Art. 7(VI)). After a decision, Art. 8 gives the customer the right to request an explanation of the specific decision, its logic and criteria, and the contestation and human-intervention mechanisms. For an AI-assisted credit decision, the bank must provide both the Art. 7 prior information and, on request, the Art. 8 decision explanation.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] Art. 7 item numbering.

question: What public transparency reporting does PL 2338/2023 require for AI systems?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 requires transparency reporting at several levels. Art. 19(II) requires, as a general governance measure, transparency about the governance measures adopted in developing and using the AI system. For high-risk systems, Art. 26 requires public disclosure of the algorithmic impact assessment conclusions (intended purpose, mitigation measures, residual risk, affected-segment participation), safeguarding trade secrets. Art. 43 requires the competent authority to maintain a public database of high-risk AI impact-assessment documents. Art. 24(1)(i) requires public transparency about residual risks, especially where there is high harm potential. A financial institution must therefore publicly report its governance measures and, for high-risk systems, publish impact-assessment conclusions accessible via the authority's database.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 address the long-term sustainability and maintenance of AI models?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 addresses model sustainability through lifecycle governance. Art. 19(1) requires governance measures to apply across the entire lifecycle from initial conception to discontinuation, and Art. 19(2) requires high-risk technical documentation to be kept updated during use. Art. 25 requires the algorithmic impact assessment to be a continuous, iterative process across the lifecycle with periodic updates. Art. 24(1)(h) requires residual-risk justification with frequent quality-control tests. Together, these require a financial institution to maintain, update, and periodically re-assess its AI models over their operational life rather than treating deployment as final — the bill's approach to sustainability is continuous governance rather than a one-time certification.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How does PL 2338/2023 handle emerging risks from an evolving fraud-detection AI, and could it become high-risk?
ground_truth: For an evolving fraud-detection AI, PL 2338/2023 handles emerging risks through notification and possible reclassification. Although fraud detection is not initially high-risk under Art. 17, Art. 18 lets the competent authority designate it high-risk if criteria such as large-scale implementation, negative impact on rights or service use, or high harm potential are met — plausible if the system increasingly blocks legitimate transactions or affects many customers. Art. 24(5) requires notifying the authority and affected persons of unexpected post-deployment risks. Art. 31 requires reporting serious incidents. So an evolving fraud AI remains lower-risk unless designated under Art. 18, but the institution must monitor for and report emerging risks, and be prepared for reclassification if the system's impact grows.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: What are the foundational responsible-AI duties a Brazilian financial institution must observe under PL 2338/2023?
ground_truth: PL 2338/2023 establishes foundational duties across all risk levels. Art. 2 sets foundations including the centrality of the human person, respect for human rights and democratic values, non-discrimination, privacy and data protection, and consumer protection. Art. 3 sets principles including effective human oversight, non-discrimination, transparency and explainability, reliability, accountability, precaution, and proportionality. Art. 19 translates these into baseline governance measures applicable to all AI agents: transparency in human-machine interaction, transparency about governance, bias-mitigation data management, LGPD-compliant data processing, proper data separation for training/testing/validation, and information security across the lifecycle. Every financial institution deploying AI — regardless of risk tier — must observe these foundational duties, with enhanced obligations added for high-risk systems.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31].

question: How do PL 2338/2023's obligations for credit-scoring AI compare with the EU AI Act and Korean AI Basic Act for a multinational bank?
ground_truth: For credit-scoring AI, PL 2338/2023, the EU AI Act, and the Korean AI Basic Act converge on classifying it as their highest regulated tier — high-risk under PL 2338 Art. 17(V), high-risk under EU Annex III Art. 5(b), and High-Impact under Korean Art. 2(4). All three impose human oversight, transparency/explanation, documentation, risk management, and impact-assessment duties (PL 2338 Art. 22; EU Art. 27 FRIA and Art. 9 risk management; Korean Art. 35). They diverge on penalties: PL 2338 up to BRL 50M or 2% of turnover (Art. 36); EU up to EUR 35M or 7%; Korea up to KRW 30M. PL 2338 uniquely imposes strict civil liability for high-risk systems (Art. 27(1)). A multinational bank can build a common high-risk control baseline (oversight, explanation, documentation, impact assessment) but must reconcile differing penalty exposures, liability regimes, and the fact that PL 2338 is not yet enacted.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31] cross-framework claims; this is the multi-jurisdiction summary item.

question: Provide an integrated summary of a Brazilian bank's core compliance obligations for a high-risk financial AI under PL 2338/2023.
ground_truth: Under PL 2338/2023, a Brazilian bank's core compliance roadmap for a high-risk financial AI (e.g., credit scoring under Art. 17(V)) is: (1) conduct and document a preliminary risk assessment (Art. 13); (2) implement general governance measures (Art. 19) — transparency, bias-mitigation data management, LGPD-compliant processing, data separation, information security, and technical documentation prepared before deployment; (3) implement enhanced high-risk measures (Art. 20) — lifecycle documentation, automatic operation-logging, reliability testing (robustness, accuracy, precision, coverage), bias mitigation with an inclusive team, explainability, and effective human oversight; (4) conduct a mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (Art. 22) by qualified, functionally independent professionals (Art. 23) following the Art. 24 methodology, updated continuously (Art. 25); (5) notify the competent authority and publish impact-assessment conclusions (Arts. 22, 26, 43); (6) honor affected-person rights (Chapter II: information, explanation, contestation, human review); (7) report serious incidents (Art. 31); and (8) recognize strict civil liability (Art. 27(1)) and potential sanctions up to BRL 50M/2% of turnover (Art. 36). Note that PL 2338 is not yet enacted; obligations apply once it becomes law.
notes: [author-verified against official Senate text 2026-07-31]. Summary/roadmap item integrating the full high-risk obligation set.
